A1.goal: Understand a few simple facts and recognise the speaker’s feelings.

gist.title: Why is the actor standing in front of this audience?
options: To speak after getting a prize
To explain a school lesson
To introduce a new film
gist.why: He is speaking at an awards ceremony.

gist.title: Which feeling can listeners hear when he mentions other people?
options: Anger
Gratitude
Fear
gist.why: He thanks people warmly throughout the speech.

detail.title: Which number does he use for the things important to him every day?
options: Two
Four
Three
detail.why: He introduces three things that guide him.

detail.title: Which relative is watching the ceremony that evening?
options: His mother
His grandfather
His uncle
detail.why: He mentions his mother in the audience.

detail.title: What kind of person does he want his children to see?
options: Someone famous for spending money
A father they can feel proud of
Someone who never needs advice
detail.why: He hopes his children can be proud of their father.

sequence: First, he shows respect for other actors.
Next, he speaks about people close to him.
Later, he remembers his idea of a hero.

facts.title: Write the number of children the speaker mentions.

open.title: In one sentence, say why his family matters to him.
open.answer: He loves his family and wants his children to be proud of him.
open.criteria: Accept a clear, relevant personal message supported by the recording.

A2.goal: Follow the main message, identify key people and understand a few exact details.

gist.title: What is the speech about besides receiving an award?
options: How to become a film director
People who matter to him and ideas for life
The history of the ceremony
gist.why: He moves from thanks to family values and personal motivation.

gist.title: What makes the speech feel friendly?
options: A mixture of thanks and jokes
A long list of film prices
A formal lesson about acting
gist.why: Personal thanks and humour create a warm atmosphere.

detail.title: What does he imagine his late father doing?
options: Watching a football game
Cooking a small breakfast
Enjoying a pot of gumbo

detail.title: What did he learn at home about respecting others?
options: It starts with respecting yourself
Only older people deserve respect
Respect has little to do with how we behave
detail.why: He connects self-respect with respect for others.

detail.title: What happens to his goal after another ten years?
options: He forgets his old ambition
He moves the ideal person into the future again
He decides that being famous is enough
detail.why: He still wants to become a better version of himself.

sequence: He thanks colleagues connected with his film.
He remembers his father in an affectionate way.
He recalls a question from his teenage years.

facts.title: What is the first name of the person he married?

open.title: Why does he tell a funny memory during a serious ceremony?
open.answer: To make the tribute personal and connect with listeners.
open.criteria: Accept a coherent explanation referring to humour or connection.

B1.goal: Follow a personal narrative, recognise supporting details and explain a central idea.

gist.title: What can listeners learn from the personal story at the end?
options: A goal may continue to guide us as we grow
Adults must stop setting new goals
Career awards bring an end to learning
Teenagers should avoid big ambitions
gist.why: The hero stays a future ideal rather than an achieved target.

gist.title: What is the effect of moving from colleagues to family memories?
options: The speaker forgets his professional role
It turns a public thank-you into a personal story
The speech becomes only about his childhood
He changes the subject to promote a new film
gist.why: He broadens the acceptance speech from film work to personal values.

detail.title: Why does he speak positively about other performers before describing his own beliefs?
options: He hopes they will give him another role
He wants to avoid talking about his family
He recognises that the honour takes place among talented colleagues
He is explaining the rules for choosing a winner
detail.why: He acknowledges fellow performers rather than claiming exclusive credit.

detail.title: What lesson does the story about his mother support?
options: Respect begins with how people value themselves
Children should accept any opinion they hear
People become successful only by following parents
The audience should think less about other people
detail.why: The family lesson links confidence and respectful behaviour.

detail.title: How does the remembered conversation about a hero end?
options: With a decision to change careers
With a warning not to dream too far ahead
With the discovery that he has already reached his ideal
With the idea that his ideal self remains ahead of him
detail.why: He continues to chase the person he hopes to become.

sequence: He credits people from the film world.
He introduces three daily guides.
He recalls a family memory.
He tells a story from adolescence.

facts.title: At what age did somebody first ask who his hero was?

open.title: Explain how one family example supports a wider message in the speech.
open.answer: The speaker turns a memory about family into a point about gratitude, self-respect or motivation.
open.criteria: Accept accurate links between a family memory and a broader idea, not a generic summary.

B2.goal: Identify detail and argument, trace the structure and interpret tone and purpose.

gist.title: Which description of the speech's development is most convincing?
options: It remains a formal list of thanks
It shifts from recognition to an explanation of personal values
It rejects the idea that cinema matters
It argues that awards have no meaning
gist.why: The address combines acknowledgement with values and a life lesson.

gist.title: What unites the examples about family and the final ambition?
options: They show how personal relationships and ideals shape the speaker
They explain how films are financed
They prove success is a result of competition alone
They suggest every ambition has a fixed deadline
gist.why: Both family and the future ideal are part of his view of identity.

detail.title: Why can the imagined scene involving his father make the tribute more effective?
options: It replaces an emotional memory with an unrelated joke
It makes the ceremony appear informal and unimportant
It combines affection with a vivid, humorous picture
It proves the speaker knew exactly what his father would do
detail.why: The sensory image gives warmth and humour to remembrance.

detail.title: What does his example about gratitude suggest?
options: Appreciating what we have can shape what follows
Gratitude matters only after professional success
People should publicly thank everyone they know
Being grateful prevents further disappointment
detail.why: He presents gratitude as a way of approaching opportunities.

detail.title: Why is the future hero never completely reached?
options: The speaker regrets his younger ambitions
He finds that his former goals no longer interest him
He is unwilling to accept his present achievements
The ideal becomes a continuing reason to improve
detail.why: He moves the ideal self forward and values ongoing effort.

sequence: He speaks with respect about his peers.
He describes the principles he needs in daily life.
He gives an affectionate picture of his father.
He returns to a long-standing personal ambition.

facts.title: Write the director's surname as mentioned in the speech.

open.title: How does the speaker combine serious feeling with humour? Use a moment from the speech.
open.answer: His tribute to his father uses an amusing imagined scene while communicating real affection.
open.criteria: Accept another well-supported contrast between sincere emotion and a joke.

C1.goal: Analyse rhetorical choices, implied values and the speaker’s construction of a public persona.

gist.title: What role does the acceptance speech play beyond celebrating a prize?
options: It publicly constructs values and a sense of identity
It rejects the usefulness of public ceremonies
It critiques the careers of the other nominees
It outlines a future film production
gist.why: The speaker uses a ceremonial honour to describe who he hopes to be.

gist.title: Which relationship between public success and personal aspiration emerges?
options: The award proves his personal work is complete
Success is acknowledged while self-development remains unfinished
He suggests ambition should end at the ceremony
Professional recognition is treated as a family obligation
gist.why: The fixed award contrasts with a self-renewing ideal.

detail.title: Why can naming colleagues be rhetorically important?
options: It delays the start of the speech without adding meaning
It turns the occasion into a competition
It situates the speaker's honour within a shared professional achievement
It makes the later family stories irrelevant
detail.why: Acknowledgements temper self-focus and recognise the wider professional community.

detail.title: How does his account of a parent challenge a uniformly solemn tribute?
options: By introducing comic detail without denying emotion
By avoiding any mention of the person he remembers
By suggesting family relationships are always simple
By presenting a strictly chronological biography
detail.why: The father is remembered through warmth and imagined humour.

detail.title: What does the repeated shift of his ideal self into the future imply?
options: The ideal was never important to him
The remembered exchange is historically inaccurate
He thinks age determines a person's worth
Self-development is framed as continuing rather than finally complete
detail.why: The story values the pursuit rather than a completed endpoint.

sequence: He recognises professional peers.
He offers a framework for his values.
He moves into his father's memory.
He uses an extended anecdote to describe ambition.

facts.title: How many years older is the ideal person in the speaker's story?

open.title: Evaluate how personal disclosure helps the speaker build an image of himself.
open.answer: He balances professional status with gratitude, faith, family affection and a never-finished ideal.
open.criteria: Look for one supported rhetorical effect and a reference to a specific passage.

C2.goal: Evaluate the speech’s argumentative tensions, identity work, rhetorical patterning and alternative interpretations.

gist.title: Which paradox best defines the speaker's closing self-portrait?
options: He seeks private success while refusing public attention
An achieved external honour accompanies a perpetually unfinished inner project
His family values contradict his claims about ambition
He celebrates a prize while dismissing his professional peers
gist.why: The acceptance of an award and the unreachable future hero sit in productive tension.

gist.title: How is the speaker's authority assembled across the address?
options: By presenting professional recognition alongside carefully selected intimate memories
By keeping a strict distance from listeners
By turning every acknowledgement into an argument about status
By denying the importance of rhetorical organisation
gist.why: Achievement, gratitude, humour and private memories jointly construct the public persona.

detail.title: Why is the imagined father scene more than a moment of comic relief?
options: It is evidence about the precise circumstances of his father's death
It changes the subject before the audience can respond
It gives absence a sensory form without abandoning affectionate humour
It displaces the personal element of the entire speech
detail.why: The vivid image allows remembrance, loss and warmth to coexist.

detail.title: What is the tension in presenting gratitude as an almost scientific principle?
options: A subjective moral view is offered with the force of a general law
The speaker claims his family produced scientific evidence
He abandons emotion to adopt a purely empirical register
The reference makes the hero anecdote impossible to interpret
detail.why: The rhetoric lifts a personal belief into a claim with broad scope.

detail.title: What role does the moving hero play in his account of achievement?
options: It proves the award should have been given later
It makes success dependent on the audience's approval
It denies that younger people can set useful goals
It reframes an unfulfilled ideal as the engine of continued aspiration
detail.why: Not reaching the ideal is presented as motivation, not straightforward failure.

sequence: The speaker identifies members of the professional community.
He lays out a recurring organising principle.
He introduces a vivid memory of his father.
He concludes through a story about the self he continues to pursue.

facts.title: Give both ages at which the person in the anecdote asks the hero question.
facts.criteria: Both ages must be present: 15 and 25.

open.title: Discuss one productive tension between personal conviction and public persuasion in the speech.
open.answer: Private values are expressed as shared lessons; humour and ceremonial ethos help reach listeners who may not share every belief.
open.criteria: Accept nuanced supported interpretations, including critical ones.
